title: Readmissions, Observation, and the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program
finding: Readmissions for the targeted conditions fell from 21.5% to 17.8% between 2007 and 2015. Observation stays grew, but hospitals with bigger readmission drops did not show bigger observation growth.

title: Association Between Hospital Penalty Status Under the HRRP and Readmission Rates for Target and Nontarget Conditions
finding: Hospitals that were later penalized cut readmissions faster than others after the program was announced. The improvement leveled off once penalties began in October 2012.

title: Mandated report: The effects of the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program
finding: Congress's advisers concluded the program lowered readmissions without a material rise in ER visits, observation stays, or deaths, saving Medicare roughly $1.5 billion a year by 2016. They suggested accounting for hospitals' low-income patient share.

cite: Ibrahim et al., JAMA Intern Med 2018
title: Association of Coded Severity With Readmission Reduction After the HRRP
finding: In this research letter, about 63% of the risk-adjusted decline was statistically attributable to rising coded severity at exposed hospitals. The authors could not tell whether the coding change was appropriate.

cite: Sabbatini et al., JAMA Netw Open 2022
title: Accounting for the Growth of Observation Stays in the Assessment of Medicare's HRRP
finding: Counting observation stays as returns cut the measured drop for targeted conditions from 1.48 to 0.66 points. The program's extra effect over non-targeted conditions was no longer statistically significant.

cite: Wright et al., Health Serv Res 2023
title: Medicare's hospital readmissions reduction program and the rise in observation stays
finding: Observation use rose only slightly faster for targeted conditions after the program began; most of the growth tracked other forces, such as billing audits.

title: Decreases In Readmissions Credited To Medicare's Program To Reduce Hospital Readmissions Have Been Overstated
finding: A change in billing standards at the same time let hospitals list more diagnoses per claim, which lowered risk-adjusted readmission rates. Accounting for it cut the measured decline for targeted conditions by 48%, and after further adjustment that decline matched two control groups.

title: Association of HRRP Implementation With Readmission and Mortality Outcomes in Heart Failure
finding: In a registry of 416 participating hospitals, with a before/after comparison and no control group, 30-day readmissions fell from 20.0% to 18.4% while 30-day deaths rose from 7.2% to 8.6% after penalties began. The authors called for confirmation.

title: Association of the HRRP With Mortality Among Medicare Beneficiaries Hospitalized for Heart Failure, AMI, and Pneumonia
finding: Across 8.3 million hospitalizations, deaths within 30 days after discharge rose for heart failure and pneumonia, mostly among patients who were never readmitted, and fell for heart attack. Deaths within 45 days of admission did not change significantly. The authors called for more research.

cite: Khera et al., JAMA Netw Open 2018
title: Association of the HRRP With Mortality During and After Hospitalization for AMI, Heart Failure, and Pneumonia
finding: Looking at the same three conditions, this team found no change in mortality trends when the program was announced or started. Heart failure deaths after discharge were already rising before the program.

title: Association of Changing Hospital Readmission Rates With Mortality Rates After Hospital Discharge
finding: In a hospital-level study of Medicare patients with heart failure, heart attack, or pneumonia from 2008 to 2014, hospitals whose readmissions fell tended to see deaths after discharge fall too, though the link was weak. The authors said this does not support rising deaths from cutting readmissions.

theme: Is it fair to safety-net hospitals?
cite: Joynt Maddox et al., JAMA Intern Med 2019
title: Association of Stratification by Dual Enrollment Status With Financial Penalties in the HRRP
finding: Comparing actual FY2018 and FY2019 penalties, the peer-group change cut penalties about $22 million for hospitals with the most dual-eligible patients and raised them about $12 million for those with the fewest.

theme: Is it fair to safety-net hospitals?
title: Three-Year Impact Of Stratification In The Medicare HRRP
finding: After three years, peer grouping lowered penalties modestly at hospitals with many dual-eligible, rural, Black, or Hispanic patients. The authors called it a modest step toward equity.

cite: Oseran et al., Ann Intern Med 2023
title: Effect of Medicare Advantage on Hospital Readmission and Mortality Rankings
finding: When Medicare Advantage patients were added to the measures, about one in four top-ranked hospitals dropped to a lower rank, while a similar share of the lowest-ranked rose. Hospitals with more Medicare Advantage patients tended to improve. Under CMS's FY2026 rule, FY2027 is the first payment year built this way.

cite: Chopra et al., JAMA Netw Open 2026
title: Hospital Readmission Reduction Program Penalties for Hospitals With High Medicare Advantage Penetration
finding: Using FY2019–FY2022 data, adjusting for local Medicare Advantage enrollment would have shifted roughly $284–297 million a year in penalties among hospitals.
